# File Handling

In these tasks, open files using the `with` statement, and for text files specify the encoding explicitly (`encoding="utf-8"`).

## Text Files

1. Create a file `hello.txt` and write three lines of text to it (mode `"w"`, method `.write()`). Remember the newline characters `"\n"`. Then open the file in mode `"r"`, read its entire contents with the `.read()` method and print them.

2. Open the file `hello.txt` from the previous task in mode `"a"` and append two new lines at its end. Print the contents of the file and check whether the previous lines have been preserved. In a comment, describe the difference between the modes `"w"`, `"a"` and `"x"`.

3. Read the file `hello.txt` line by line by iterating directly over the file object, and print each line preceded by its number. Remove the newline characters with the `.rstrip("\n")` method to avoid empty lines in the output.

4. Compare how the `.read()`, `.readline()` and `.readlines()` methods work on the same file. Check the type of the returned result in each case.

5. Read successive names from the user (until an empty string is entered) and save them in the file `names.txt` — each on a separate line — using the `.writelines()` method.

6. Write a function `file_stats(path)` that returns a tuple with the number of lines, the number of words and the number of characters in a text file (similar to the `wc` command on Unix systems). Test it on a file of your choice.

7. Write a program that tries to open a file whose name is given by the user and prints its contents. If the file does not exist, catch the `FileNotFoundError` exception and print an appropriate message.

8. Create a file `numbers.txt` containing integers on successive lines (some lines may be empty or contain text that is not a number). Write a program that reads the file, skips invalid lines (handling the `ValueError` exception) and prints the sum, minimum, maximum and the number of skipped lines.

9. Write a function `count_words(path)` that returns a dictionary with the number of occurrences of each word in a text file. Convert all letters to lowercase and remove the punctuation characters `.,;:!?`. Print the 10 most frequent words (hint: `sorted(counts, key=counts.get, reverse=True)`).

10. Write a function `copy_uppercase(source, target)` that copies the text file `source` to the file `target`, converting all letters to uppercase. Open both files in a single `with` statement.

11. Given the file `grades.csv` with the following contents:
```
name;math;physics;computer_science
Alice;5;4;5
Bob;3;4;4
Charlie;4;5;3
Diana;5;5;5
```
Read the file without using any additional modules (the `.strip()` and `.split(";")` methods), skip the header row and print the average grade for each person. Then save the names and averages (rounded to two decimal places) to the file `averages.csv`.

12. Solve the previous task again, this time using the `csv` module (`csv.reader` with the parameter `delimiter=";"` and `csv.writer`). When opening the file for writing, use the parameter `newline=""`.

13. Write a function `save_contacts(contacts, path)` that saves a dictionary of contacts `{name: phone number}` to a text file in the form `name=number` (each contact on a separate line), and a function `load_contacts(path)` that reads such a file and returns a dictionary. Check that after saving and loading you get a dictionary equal to the original one.

14. Save the same dictionary of contacts to the file `contacts.json` using the `json.dump()` function (with the parameters `ensure_ascii=False` and `indent=2`) and read it back with the `json.load()` function. Open the file in a text editor and compare its contents with the file from the previous task.

15. Write a journal program: each time it is run, it reads one line of text from the user and appends it to the end of the file `journal.txt` together with the number of the entry (determine the number by counting the existing lines of the file; take into account the case where the file does not exist yet).

## Binary Files

16. Create a `bytes` object using `bytes([72, 101, 108, 108, 111])` and print it. Then encode the string `"Zażółć gęślą jaźń"` (a Polish phrase full of diacritics) into bytes with the `.encode("utf-8")` method, and print the number of characters in the string and the number of bytes after encoding. In a comment, explain the difference.

17. Write the string `"Zażółć gęślą jaźń"` to a text file with `utf-8` encoding, then open this file in binary mode `"rb"` and print its contents as a `bytes` object as well as a list of the values of successive bytes (`list(data)`). Also try reading the file in text mode with the `cp1250` encoding (a legacy Central European Windows code page) and describe the result.

18. Write the numbers from 0 to 255 as successive bytes to the binary file `data.bin` (mode `"wb"`). Read the file, check its size (`len()`) and print the bytes at indices 65 to 90. Decode them into a string and explain the result.

19. Write the integers `[1, 300, 70000, -5]` to a binary file, converting each of them into 4 bytes with the `int.to_bytes(4, "little", signed=True)` method. Then read the file 4 bytes at a time (`.read(4)`) and reconstruct the numbers with the `int.from_bytes()` method.

20. Write a function `copy_binary(source, target, chunk_size=4096)` that copies any file (e.g. a JPG image) in binary mode, reading it in chunks of size `chunk_size` in a `while` loop. Check whether the copy is identical to the original by comparing the contents of both files read in binary mode.

21. PNG files start with the 8-byte signature `b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"`, and JPEG files start with the bytes `b"\xff\xd8\xff"`. Write a function `detect_image_type(path)` that reads the beginning of a file and returns `"PNG"`, `"JPEG"` or `"unknown"`. Test it on several files, including a text file.

22. Open the file `data.bin` from task 18 in mode `"rb"`. Using the `.seek()` method, move to the byte at index 100, read 5 bytes and print them. Then print the current position in the file using the `.tell()` method.
